name: Tara Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a small dozer at a large mine and level the ground where the haul trucks turn. I am 43, and I still ask a senior operator to look over the harder edges; reading the ground takes longer to learn than the levers. Our two children are in school, my partner Jules repairs bicycles, and there is a mortgage to pay. The mine pays me well enough that we have saved more than six months of expenses, though I remember the years when we had almost nothing left after payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my crew that a little office automation is fine if it doesn't excuse skipping a proper ground check. I use an AI tool now and then to put a technical term into ordinary words, but a more experienced operator still checks my dozer work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, this sounds like the mine we've already got, and I expect my own shifts to hold. Jules has steady repair orders at the moment, and our savings are large enough to cover more than half a year of bills. I'd still want the union to watch any quiet change to staffing. A small software saving can hide a staffing cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the dozer shifts and walk the turning area before I start a cut. At our next union meeting I'd ask whether the office has changed the way it counts crew hours. In the first year I wouldn't move the children or take on another bill because of this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our money and my work here. The part that nags me is how easily a small change gets hidden in a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a ground check catch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Water can soften the edge overnight, and a wheel mark can tell you a truck came too close yesterday. I look for both before the first load comes around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union for such a small change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We can ask one question now without turning it into a fight. It is harder to find the missing hours after the rota has already been rewritten.

say: I would say **minor office automation** must not replace a proper ground check.
I use an AI tool occasionally, while a **senior operator** still checks difficult dozer work.
think: I expect **my shifts** and Jules’s repair orders to hold in this mild picture.
Our **six-month cushion** gives us room, though staffing changes still deserve scrutiny.
do: Keep the **dozer shifts** and walk the truck turning area before each cut.
Ask at the next **union meeting** whether office changes affect crew hours.
feel: **Calm** about family income, with a watchful eye on hidden roster changes.
S0.quote: A small software saving can hide a staffing cut.
fieldNote: Tara’s savings and current work make her **financially calm** under a mild change.
Her union question comes from earlier lean years and concern that **small software savings** can hide staffing cuts.

steps.text: Keep driving the dozer and walk the turning area before cuts
Ask the union whether office changes alter crew hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the mine's planners and buyers will feel this before my dozer does. The crew should see any new roster and have someone accountable for the route decisions, because the ground doesn't become dry just because a computer says it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still junior, so I could be the person sent home if faster planning means one fewer shift. We have savings and other mines nearby, but the higher wage here pays our mortgage and gives the children a steady week. I have used AI enough to know a tidy answer can still be wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask a senior operator to show me the updated digital route map after they have tested it on the ground. Then I'd use the map with my own walk around, and ask the union representative for the old and new shift counts. If my hours shrink in the first year, I'd apply to two other mines nearby before drawing on savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about a better map but anxious about the junior roster. I can handle learning a tool; I cannot make a missing paid day harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you compare on the maps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the drainage line and the turning radius with the marks I can see under my boots. A map that misses water is no help to a truck driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you apply elsewhere?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the first real cut to my roster, not after a rumour. Jules and I would look at the travel time so a new mine didn't strand the children after school.

say: I would say **planners and buyers** feel the change before dozer operators.
I want visible **rosters and routes** for the crew.
think: A junior operator could lose **a paid shift** if planning becomes leaner.
Nearby mines and savings help, but this **higher wage** supports the mortgage.
do: Test the **digital route map** with a senior operator and a ground walk.
Request old and new **shift counts** through the union.
Apply to **two nearby mines** if my roster actually shrinks.
feel: Curious about the map, but **anxious** about lost junior hours.
S1.quote: A map that misses water is no help to a truck driver.
fieldNote: Tara will use a tool once an experienced operator has **tested it** against the actual ground.
Her first response to fewer hours is an **application**, made possible by plentiful nearby mines.

steps.text: Test the AI route map with a senior operator and a ground walk
Request old and new shift counts through the union
Apply to two nearby mines if the roster shrinks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the union that the thinking jobs change in 2028 but a dozer that works like a person comes around 2031. Three years of driving isn't a promise of a job after that. We need paid training places and a clear count of the equipment the mine plans to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm scared of losing the wage before the mortgage is small enough to carry on Jules's bicycle repair income. The children will still be at school in 2031, and more than six months saved will not pay for years without work. I'm willing to learn, but I'm junior at this job already and can't pretend to be a qualified fitter by next Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go with the union representative to ask for a written robot purchase timetable and paid training slots. I'd keep the dozer shifts while they exist, and ask the maintenance lead whether a supervised inspection place is open. In 2029 I'd apply for one if the pay covers our basic bills, and I'd apply to nearby mines still hiring operators if it doesn't. Once capable robots arrive in 2031, I'd use whichever paid job I had secured rather than wait for my old seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels frighteningly quick, but I do have people and savings to help me act. The hard part is trusting a training offer when no wage is written beside it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why inspection rather than another driving seat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A driving seat at a second mine might disappear on the same timetable. Inspection could buy a different kind of paid experience, though robots may change that work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Jules tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the mortgage statement on the table and explain the two dates. Jules would ask what a trainee actually earns before we promised the children anything different.

say: I would explain **2028 AI** and **2031 dozers** as separate dates.
I would demand **paid training** and an equipment purchase count.
think: Losing my higher wage could leave the **mortgage** beyond Jules’s repair income.
Six months of savings would not cover **years without work** while children remain in school.
do: Ask through the union for a **robot timetable** and paid training slots.
Keep driving and ask about **supervised inspection** work.
Apply in 2029 for a paid place or **nearby operator jobs** if wages fail.
feel: **Frightened** by the speed, while able to use savings and contacts.
S2.quote: Three years of driving isn't a promise of a job after that.
fieldNote: Tara understands the **three-year gap** as a chance to secure wages, not a permanent shelter.
Her willingness to retrain depends on **written pay** that can cover the family’s basic bills.

steps.text: Ask the union for a robot purchase timetable and paid training slots
Keep the dozer shifts while driving work exists
Apply in 2029 for supervised inspection if pay covers basic bills
Apply to nearby mines if the paid training wage is insufficient

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the mine time to show a real plan and gives workers time to challenge it. The office can change under AGI in 2031, but our dozers become replaceable by capable robots around 2034. I'd want a place for drivers in every yearly review.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the thinking work changes and 51 when robots reach the dozer. The children will be older, but I won't count their education costs as zero; the mortgage might still be there too. With nearby mines and a good savings cushion, I can try a paid inspection path without selling the house in a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union to bargain for one paid inspection placement each year for junior operators, not just senior people. I would visit the maintenance shed and ask the lead what skills a trainee must show. If a paid placement appears, I'd enrol while keeping my current shifts where possible. In 2032 I'd check whether driver hours are falling and send applications to other mines if they are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel cautious but less pressed than in the fast picture. Five years lets me see whether the training actually leads to work before I put the mortgage at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the maintenance lead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether a beginner can learn to inspect brakes and tyres under supervision, and what the first month's wage is. I'm happy to practise, but I won't call an unpaid visit a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Jules want you to leave the mine?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules would want the written offer on the kitchen table first. We can take some risk, but our children need the school week to stay predictable.

say: I would say **five years** permits a mine plan that workers can challenge.
I want **drivers included** in yearly robot reviews through 2034.
think: At 51, I may have **children and mortgage** rather than a free household budget.
My savings and nearby mines make a **paid inspection path** possible.
do: Ask the union for **paid junior placements** in inspection.
Visit maintenance and enrol if a **paid trainee place** appears.
Check 2032 driver hours and apply **elsewhere** if they fall.
feel: **Cautious**, with enough time to test whether training leads to wages.
S3.quote: I won't call an unpaid visit a new career.
fieldNote: Tara wants junior operators included because **senior-first training** would leave her behind.
Her risk tolerance has a clear boundary: a **written paid offer** must preserve the children’s routine.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid junior inspection placements
Enrol in supervised inspection if a paid trainee place appears
Apply to other mines in 2032 if driver hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell people a decade is long enough for the mine to publish milestones instead of rumours. Thinking AI arrives in 2036 and robots that can drive or grade as well as us around 2039. We should bargain early, while our current skills still have value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 in 2036 and 56 in 2039, I cannot assume I'll be retired. Our children should be grown and the school fees behind us, but I don't know what the mortgage balance or Jules's shop income will be. A decade lets me build inspection experience while I still draw a mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd ask the union to put robot purchasing and paid vacancies on its regular agenda. I'd use the mine's tested digital route system when a senior operator signs off on it, and save a fixed amount from each higher wage payment for a later job change. In 2037 I'd still drive the dozer and apply for a paid inspection shift if one opened. Before 2039 I'd compare those wages with other local mines rather than wait for the robot to take my machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel prepared enough to work on a plan, not secure enough to forget it. A decade can be used well or quietly wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you set the savings amount?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules and I would agree on an amount after the mortgage and ordinary bills, then automate that transfer on pay day. I won't use the children's current school money to make a retirement story sound tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the mine never offers inspection shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply to a nearby pit that does. There are several within reach, and I can compare actual wages without moving the family.

say: I would ask the mine for **published milestones** before robots reach the dozers.
I would bargain while our **current skills** still carry value.
think: At 56, I cannot assume **retirement** replaces my wages.
Grown children may cost less, while the **mortgage and shop income** remain uncertain.
do: Put **robot purchases and vacancies** on the union agenda.
Use the tested route system and save a **fixed wage amount**.
Drive in 2037 and apply for **paid inspection shifts** before 2039.
feel: **Prepared to plan**, without assuming lifelong job security.
S4.quote: A decade can be used well or quietly wasted.
fieldNote: The ten-year runway lets Tara pair **tested technology** with a steady savings habit.
She treats retirement and Jules’s future shop income as **unknowns**, despite a strong current cushion.

steps.text: Put robot orders and paid vacancies on the union agenda
Use the tested digital route system after senior signoff
Transfer a fixed amount from each higher wage payment
Apply for paid inspection shifts before 2039

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because the three-year gap is short for a junior operator to earn a new skill. Written trainee wages, a real place to practise, and a public purchase timetable would help. Our savings give us breathing room, but they aren't a wage forever.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how junior people get picked for training. If only the longest-serving drivers get offered a place, the rest of us lose the very time we're supposed to use. A training list should show who got in and why.

headlineQuote: A training list should show who got in and why.
portrait: Tara is a **43-year-old junior dozer operator** who checks difficult ground with senior colleagues.
Her **higher wage and savings** buffer risk, while two school-age children and a mortgage shape every training choice.
She tries new tools after **ground testing**, and uses union questions to demand visible rosters and fair placements.
She sees the **robot lag** as time for paid inspection experience rather than guaranteed mining work.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, with capable mining robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Written trainee wages**, supervised places and a public robot purchase timetable would let junior workers plan.
